title: MARL-BattleGrounds: A Novel JAX-native Benchmark for Heterogeneous and Competitive Multi-agent RL

paper.title: MARL-BattleGrounds: A Novel JAX-native Benchmark for Heterogeneous and Competitive Multi-agent RL
paper.abstract: Abstract. We present MARL-BattleGrounds (MARL-BGs), an easy-to-use JAX-native benchmark for heterogeneous and competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), designed to be sample-efficient, computationally efficient, and researcher-centric. MARL benchmarks are typically simple and efficient, like SMAX, where winning reduces to unit micromanagement, or rich and costly, like Dota 2. MARL-BGs fills this missing middle. Its first mode, Team Deathmatch, is a simultaneous turn-based game between two teams of five heterogeneous agents. The five classes have distinct basic, passive, and ultimate abilities designed to synergize with allies and counter enemies. Our 52 hand-designed maps with diverse obstacles include a 12-map curriculum and ten held-out validation and test maps. MARL-BGs provides two canonical evaluation modes. First, eight endgame scenarios form a hard generalization challenge: each asks a team to win an unseen, nearly lost position against a strong reactive controller within 5--10 ticks, testing agent modeling, multi-step planning, and more. Second, a monthly round-robin tournament retrains each submission on equal compute, plays it against every member of the current ‘‘Big Nine’’ field, and publishes the Elo results on the official leaderboard. All entrants are publicly released as downloadable opponents. To help researchers train and evaluate their policies, MARL-BGs records 11,192 metrics per game in 28 topics, from damage and healing to team coordination and formation. We also include three strong scripted opponents, an analytical replay viewer, and off-the-shelf tools for self-play, cross-play, curriculum learning, and zero-shot coordination evaluation. We even provide an API for LLM-based agents and use it to evaluate Qwen3.5-9B against our strongest policy. In our BattleClient, human researchers can play alongside or against any mix of policies, enabling human-AI evaluation. We benchmark MARL-BGs with six additional deep MARL baselines, which we release. On one RTX 5090 with 1,024 parallel games, the simulator runs 50,000 5v5 game steps per second. To our knowledge, no other MARL benchmark offers this breadth and depth of research and evaluation tools. 1 1 1 Everything there is to know about MARL-BGs is available on our website ( \weblink https://marl-battlegrounds.commarl-battlegrounds.com), including interactive demos and comprehensive tutorials, and the full GitHub repository and Hugging Face models will be made public upon manuscript acceptance.

Keywords: Multi-agent reinforcement learning, Benchmark, JAX, Heterogeneous agents, Team competition, Evaluation 1. Introduction Many multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) benchmarks sit at two extremes. At one end are fast and simple benchmarks such as SMAX ( Rutherford et al., 2024 ) , which runs StarCraft-style unit battles on the GPU in JAX, but its units only move and shoot and differ only in stats such as health, speed, and range, so winning reduces to low-level unit micromanagement. At the other end are full games such as Dota 2. Dota 2 demands deep coordination among specialist agents, and it took OpenAI Five ten months of training on large GPU and CPU clusters to reach the final agent performance ( OpenAI et al., 2019 ) . Few research groups can run experiments at that scale, and iterating over results makes improvements difficult. That leaves a missing middle. The middle matters because central questions in MARL need both rich team play and fast, cheap experiments: how agents with different abilities share what they learn, how a team assigns credit for a heal or a stun that pays off only through a teammate, how teammates time their actions together, and whether the resulting policies still work with opponents and teammates they never met. Evaluation has three gaps of its own. Fixed tasks get solved: by 2021, the best published win rates on most popular SMAC ( Samvelyan et al., 2019 ) maps were close to 100% ( Gorsane et al., 2022 ) , and SMACv2 found that policies which ignore their observations still win many SMAC tasks ( Ellis et al., 2023 ) . Results are hard to compare: re-analyzed ( Gorsane et al., 2022 ) on 6 of SMAC’s 14 maps, a common choice, QMIX ( Rashid et al., 2018 ) lost its lead over VDN ( Sunehag et al., 2018 ) , and in Google Research Football an agent trained against a frozen earlier agent beat it but played poorly against the built-in bot ( Kurach et al., 2020 ) , so one fixed opponent misleads. And a score hides what a team learned: in Overcooked, self-play agents worked well with each other but worse with humans, and watching their games showed why: they used one of the two pots, while humans used both ( Carroll et al., 2019 ) . We present MARL-BattleGrounds (MARL-BGs), an easy-to-use JAX-native benchmark for heterogeneous and competitive team-vs-team MARL that fills the missing middle. MARL-BGs was built on our own engine and designed to be sample-efficient, computationally efficient, and researcher-centric. Its three parts are our contributions: i) The Game , ii) The Evaluation , and iii) The Tools . i) The Game , Team Deathmatch, demands high-level team coordination from teams of up to five agents (Section 4 ). We introduce five classes, inspired by World of Warcraft, with hand-designed abilities that require agents to synergize with allies and counter enemies (Figure 2 ). The game has 52 maps with obstacles, and partial observability, requiring tight coordination from agents. ii) The Evaluation answers the three gaps (Section 5 ). We provide a monthly tournament where researchers can upload their policies and compete against other MARL policies. Every method is rated with draw-aware Elo ( Elo, 1978 ; Davidson, 1970 ) and confidence intervals on the same held-out test maps, under the same budget, in mirrored 5v5 games with spawn ends swapped, so results are comparable. The leaderboard also provides other researchers with harder policies to train against, improving the community’s ability to progress. Eight hand-crafted endgame scenarios, each with a verified winning line, test skills such as agent modeling and multi-step planning, so a failed scenario points to a missing skill. Behind every result, up to 11,192 metrics per game in 28 topics (Figure 4 ) allow us to analyze the teamwork, such as how much the Priest healed each ally, so methods can be judged by their coordination, not only by their win rates. iii) The Tools cover the whole research workflow (Section 6 ). Researchers bring their own learner through plain JAX reset and step or start from six tuned baselines, and one call evaluates any mix of policies, so cross-play and zero-shot coordination tests come out of the box. We provide three strong scripted opponents and all checkpoints of our baselines, providing researchers with opponents of all strengths. Our LLM API turns any language model into a team of agents, enabling the evaluation of foundation models. In the BattleClient, researchers play alongside or against their policies for human-AI teaming evaluation, and in the analytical Replay Viewer they step through any game tick by tick. We demonstrate every part of MARL-BGs on Season 0, its first tournament (Section 7 ). Each PPO baseline trains at about a million game steps per minute on one RTX 5090 with 512 parallel games. Recurrent IPPO, our strongest baseline, loses to all three scripted opponents at 40 million steps but wins 579 of 600 games against them at 250 million, on the held-out test maps (Figure 5 ). Our results demonstrate that stronger teams combine their abilities, yet no system solves a scenario, an LLM team plays legally but not as a team, and learned agents partner poorly with strangers and with an expert human, who also beats the tournament winner. These open problems are exactly what MARL-BGs is built to measure. 2. Related Work Table 1. Features of MARL benchmarks, grouped by family: ✓ yes, ∘ \circ partial, ✗ no.
